claims.claim: Restored egg production is associated with increased and extended exopher production, provided that hermaphrodites were mated to fertilization-proficient males.
claims.source: We found that restored egg production is associated with increased and extended exopher production, provided that hermaphrodites were mated to fertilization-proficient males (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Adult ALMR exophergenesis is driven by the presence of fertilized eggs.
claims.source: We conclude that adult ALMR exophergenesis is driven by the presence of fertilized eggs and that the older age decrease in exopher production (~Ad4) under standard culture conditions is more likely attributed to the lack of fertilized egg accumulation at this life stage, rather than to the existence of a chronological limit on the biochemical capacity to elevate exopher levels at older ages.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figure 3B showing restoration of exophers with late-life mating.

claims.claim: The older age decrease in exopher production (approximately Ad4) under standard culture conditions is more likely attributed to the lack of fertilized egg accumulation at this life stage, rather than to the existence of a chronological limit on the biochemical capacity to elevate exopher levels at older ages.
claims.source: We conclude that adult ALMR exophergenesis is driven by the presence of fertilized eggs and that the older age decrease in exopher production (~Ad4) under standard culture conditions is more likely attributed to the lack of fertilized egg accumulation at this life stage, rather than to the existence of a chronological limit on the biochemical capacity to elevate exopher levels at older ages.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The associated massive egg retention correlated with a dramatic elevation of exopher numbers for each genetic impediment to egg laying (egl-9, egl-3, sem-2, lin-39 RNAi).
claims.source: We found that the associated massive egg retention correlated with a dramatic elevation of exopher numbers for each genetic impediment to egg laying (egl-9 (Figure 3D); egl-3 (Figure 3E); sem-2 (Figure 3F), lin-39 RNAi (Figure 3G)).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3D-G.

claims.claim: Under the treatment of lin-39 RNAi, approximately 60% of the wild-type strain expressing mCherry in ALMR by a multi-copy transgene produced ALMR exophers on Ad1, compared to only approximately 7% of the same strain treated with empty vector (EV) control.
claims.source: For example, under the treatment of lin-39 RNAi, ~60% of the wild-type strain expressing mCherry in ALMR by a multi-copy transgene produced ALMR exophers on Ad1, compared to only ~7% of the same strain treated with empty vector (EV) control (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Regardless of the genetic strategy employed to trap eggs in the body, egg retention can lead to high ALMR exopher production.
claims.source: We conclude that regardless of the genetic strategy employed to trap eggs in the body, egg retention can lead to high ALMR exopher production.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figures 3D-G showing consistent effects across different egg retention mutants.

claims.claim: The empty vector control treatment without induction of egg retention is associated with no ALMR exophergenesis in the single copy mKate transgenic strain (0% in all three trials).
claims.source: We found that the empty vector control treatment without induction of egg retention is associated with no ALMR exophergenesis in the single copy mKate transgenic strain (0% in all three trials).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: When treated with lin-39 RNAi to induce egg retention, approximately 60% exophergenesis was measured in the single copy mKate transgenic strain.
claims.source: However, when we treated with lin-39 RNAi to induce egg retention, we measured ~60% exophergenesis (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: Regardless of the expression levels of exogenous proteins in the ALMR neuron, the egg retention condition can induce high exopher production.
claims.source: Thus regardless of the expression levels of exogenous proteins in the ALMR neuron, the egg retention condition can induce high exopher production.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figures 3G and 3H comparing multi-copy and single-copy transgenes.

claims.claim: Neurotransmitters octopamine (OA) and serotonin (5-HT) have been well-documented to play opposing roles in C. elegans egg-laying behavior.
claims.source: Neurotransmitters octopamine (OA) and serotonin (5-HT) have been well-documented to play opposing roles in C. elegans egg-laying behavior (Chase and Koelle, 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Chase and Koelle, 2007).

claims.claim: Feeding C. elegans octopamine strongly suppresses egg-laying to induce egg retention.
claims.source: Feeding C. elegans octopamine strongly suppresses egg-laying to induce egg retention, while supplementing with 5-HT causes hyperactive egg-laying (Horvitz et al., 1982).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Horvitz et al., 1982).

claims.claim: Supplementing with 5-HT causes hyperactive egg-laying.
claims.source: Feeding C. elegans octopamine strongly suppresses egg-laying to induce egg retention, while supplementing with 5-HT causes hyperactive egg-laying (Horvitz et al., 1982).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Horvitz et al., 1982).

claims.claim: Treatment with egg retention-promoting OA enhanced ALMR exophergenesis.
claims.source: Consistent with outcomes in animals physically blocked for egg-laying, treatment with egg retention-promoting OA enhanced ALMR exophergenesis (Figure 3I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claims.claim: 5-HT treatment, which lowers egg retention, strongly suppresses fasting-associated ALMR exophergenesis.
claims.source: We find that 5-HT treatment, which lowers egg retention, strongly suppresses fasting-associated ALMR exophergenesis (Figure 3I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claims.claim: Null allele goa-1(n1134) removes Goα inhibition such that eggs are often laid at very early developmental stages (2–4 cell stage) rather than being retained in the uterus until gastrulation (approximately 30 cell stage).
claims.source: The egg-laying circuit Is controlled in part by Goα inhibition—null allele goa-1(n1134) removes this inhibition such that eggs are often laid at very early developmental stages (2–4 cell stage) rather than being retained in the uterus until gastrulation (~30 cell stage) (Waggoner et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Waggoner et al., 2000).

claims.claim: goa-1(n1134) retains few eggs in the uterus and is associated with a significantly lower number of ALMR exopher events as compared to the age-matched wild-type control.
claims.source: We confirmed that goa-1(n1134) retains few eggs in the uterus and is associated with a significantly lower number of ALMR exopher events as compared to the age-matched wild-type control (Figure 3J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J.

claims.claim: Manipulation of uterine egg occupancy is strongly correlated with the extent of ALMR neuronal exophergenesis—high egg retention promotes high exophergenesis and low egg retention is associated with low exophergenesis.
claims.source: In sum, manipulation of uterine egg occupancy is strongly correlated with the extent of ALMR neuronal exophergenesis—high egg retention promotes high exophergenesis and low egg retention is associated with low exophergenesis.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the cumulative experimental data in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The ALML and ALMR anterior touch neurons share developmental, morphological, and functional similarities.
claims.source: The ALML and ALMR anterior touch neurons share developmental, morphological, and functional similarities (Chalfie and Sulston, 1981), yet paradoxically, ALMR consistently produces exophers at higher levels than ALML (Melentijevic et al., 2017; also Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Chalfie and Sulston, 1981).

claims.claim: ALMR consistently produces exophers at higher levels than ALML.
claims.source: The ALML and ALMR anterior touch neurons share developmental, morphological, and functional similarities (Chalfie and Sulston, 1981), yet paradoxically, ALMR consistently produces exophers at higher levels than ALML (Melentijevic et al., 2017; also Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Melentijevic et al., 2017) and experimental data in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: The ALMR soma is situated in the vicinity of the gonad and its resident eggs, whereas the ALML soma, on the opposite side of the animal, is positioned closer to the intestine.
claims.source: The ALM neurons are embedded within the C. elegans hypodermis, but the ALMR soma is situated in the vicinity of the gonad and its resident eggs, whereas the ALML soma, on the opposite side of the animal, is positioned closer to the intestine (Figure 4A and B; Goodman, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical diagrams in Figures 4A and 4B and citation (Goodman, 2006).

claims.claim: 36/37 (95%) of the Exopher+ ALMR neuronal somas that had produced exophers were positioned within the visualized egg zone.
claims.source: We found that 37/128 ALMRs examined had produced an exopher (Exopher+), and that 36/37 (95%) of the Exopher+ ALMR neuronal somas that had produced exophers were positioned within the visualized egg zone (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: For the Exopher- ALMRs that had not produced exophers, 63/91 (70%) had neuronal somas located in the egg zone.
claims.source: For the Exopher- ALMRs that had not produced exophers, 63/91 (70%) had neuronal somas located in the egg zone.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Although ALMR soma positioning in the egg zone does not guarantee exophergenesis in the mCherryAg2 strain, the neurons that did make exophers were nearly always in the egg zone (p<0.01 in Chi-Square test).
claims.source: Thus, although ALMR soma positioning in the egg zone does not guarantee exophergenesis in the mCherryAg2 strain, the neurons that did make exophers were nearly always in the egg zone (p<0.01 in Chi-Square test, Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Transgenic introduction of a mec-3 promoter fragment bearing an internal deletion (fusion of the –1 to –563 sequences to the –1898 to –2372 mec-3 promoter fragment, plasmid pJC4) can induce anterior ALM migration during development, sometimes resulting in final ALM positions anterior to AVM.
claims.source: In particular, transgenic introduction of a mec-3 promoter fragment bearing an internal deletion (fusion of the –1 to –563 sequences to the –1898 to –2372 mec-3 promoter fragment, plasmid pJC4) can induce anterior ALM migration during development, sometimes resulting in final ALM positions anterior to AVM (Toms et al., 2001; Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Toms et al., 2001).

claims.claim: Rol hermaphrodites have a strikingly high baseline of ALMR exophergenesis (approximately 40% exophers in rollers vs. approximately 20% in the wild-type).
claims.source: Rol hermaphrodites have a strikingly high baseline of ALMR exophergenesis (~40% exophers in rollers vs. ~20% in the wild-type).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations in the pJC4 + rol-6(su1006) strain.

claims.claim: When ALMs are situated anterior to AVM, ALMR exophergenesis drops to approximately 5% (4/73) vs 71% for the posterior position (55/78).
claims.source: Strikingly, we found that when ALMs are situated anterior to AVM, ALMR exophergenesis drops to ~5% (4/73) vs 71% for the posterior position (55/78) (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: In the sem-2(rf) background, every touch neuron that is positioned in the general region of the expanded uterus (ALML, AVM, PVM) increases exopher production, but the posterior PLM neurons, which cannot be approached by the gonad, do not produce exophers.
claims.source: Indeed, we find that in the sem-2(rf) background, every touch neuron that is positioned in the general region of the expanded uterus (ALML, AVM, PVM) increases exopher production, but the posterior PLM neurons, which cannot be approached by the gonad, do not produce exophers (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Touch neurons can be stimulated to produce exophers if the egg domain is artificially brought closer to them.
claims.source: Thus, touch neurons can be stimulated to produce exophers if the egg domain is artificially brought closer to them.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figure 4G showing increased exophers in multiple touch neurons when the uterus expands.

claims.claim: ALMR normally makes most exophers because of its closest natural positioning near the egg-filled uterus.
claims.source: Data are consistent with a model in which ALMR normally makes most exophers because of its closest natural positioning near the egg-filled uterus.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figure 4 showing correlation between proximity to eggs and exopher production.

claims.claim: Eggs can readily be observed to distort tissue structure in young adult C. elegans.
claims.source: Eggs can readily be observed to distort tissue structure in young adult C. elegans.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The uterus can approach and pressure surrounding tissue, including touch neurons.
claims.source: Thus, the uterus can approach and pressure surrounding tissue, including touch neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from observations in Figure 5A showing tissue distortion by eggs.

claims.claim: Egg retention mutants that exhibit high exophergenesis, egl-3(Δ), egl-9(Δ), and sem-2(rf), had significantly longer egg zones (i.e. uterus length) as compared to wild-type.
claims.source: We found that egg retention mutants that exhibit high exophergenesis, egl-3(Δ) (Figure 5B), egl-9(Δ) (Figure 5C), and sem-2(rf) (Figure 5D), had significantly longer egg zones (i.e. uterus length) as compared to wild-type.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5B-D.

claims.claim: cbd-1 RNAi, sperm-less induction with SPE-44 AID, and hyperactive egg-laying mutant goa-1(Δ), which are strong exophergenesis suppressors, are all associated with short uterine egg zones.
claims.source: In contrast, cbd-1 RNAi (Figure 5E), sperm-less induction with SPE-44 AID (Figure 5F), and hyperactive egg-laying mutant goa-1(Δ) (Figure 5G), which we find to be strong exophergenesis suppressors, are all associated with short uterine egg zones.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5E-G.

claims.claim: Knocking down either the 4 cell stage gene mex-3 or the gastrulation gene gad-1, which are associated with neither egg retention nor exopher elevation, does not have an extended egg zone/uterine length.
claims.source: Knocking down either the 4 cell stage gene mex-3 or the gastrulation gene gad-1, which are associated with neither egg retention nor exopher elevation, does not have an extended egg zone/uterine length (Figure 5H), so not all developmental compromises are associated with uterine extension.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: Not all developmental compromises are associated with uterine extension.
claims.source: Knocking down either the 4 cell stage gene mex-3 or the gastrulation gene gad-1, which are associated with neither egg retention nor exopher elevation, does not have an extended egg zone/uterine length (Figure 5H), so not all developmental compromises are associated with uterine extension.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: Under conditions of cbd-1 RNAi, eggshell development and embryonic development are blocked.
claims.source: Under conditions of cbd-1 RNAi, eggshell development and embryonic development are blocked; eggs that form are fragile and can be malformed consequent to passing through the spermatheca into the uterus; embryonic development does not proceed and egg remnants tend to be sticky (Johnston et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Johnston et al., 2010).

claims.claim: Treating WT reproductive animals (that have functional egg-laying capacity) with cbd-1 RNAi to kill embryos exerts a potent block on ALMR exophergenesis.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 2B (and again in Figure 6A), treating WT reproductive animals (that have functional egg-laying capacity) with cbd-1 RNAi to kill embryos exerts a potent block on ALMR exophergenesis.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2B and 6A.

claims.claim: cbd-1 RNAi/dead embryo retention in the sem-2(rf) background is still associated with significantly elevated levels of ALMR exophergenesis (approximately 45%), while in egg-laying proficient wild-type, barely any ALMR exophergenesis is observed under cbd-1 RNAi conditions (<1%).
claims.source: Strikingly, we found that cbd-1 RNAi/dead embryo retention in the sem-2(rf) background is still associated with significantly elevated levels of ALMR exophergenesis (~45%), while in egg-laying proficient wild-type, barely any ALMR exophergenesis is observed under cbd-1 RNAi conditions (<1%) (69/150 for sem-2 egg-laying blocked cbd-1 RNAi vs. 1/150 for egg-laying proficient cbd-1 RNAi, Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Under conditions of defective eggshell/dead embryo retention associated with cbd-1 RNAi; sem-2(rf), the uterine egg zone is expanded.
claims.source: Importantly, under conditions of defective eggshell/dead embryo retention associated with cbd-1 RNAi; sem-2(rf), the uterine egg zone is expanded (Figure 6B), extending the correlation of exopher production with uterine length.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Intact eggshells and earliest embryonic divisions are not required for the boost in exopher production observed when uterine contents are forced to accumulate.
claims.source: We conclude that intact eggshells and earliest embryonic divisions are not required for the boost in exopher production observed when uterine contents are forced to accumulate—uterine retention of dead eggs and egg remnants is sufficient for exopher elevation if the egg laying apparatus is defective.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figure 6A showing high exophers with cbd-1 RNAi in sem-2(rf) background.

claims.claim: Uterine retention of dead eggs and egg remnants is sufficient for exopher elevation if the egg laying apparatus is defective.
claims.source: We conclude that intact eggshells and earliest embryonic divisions are not required for the boost in exopher production observed when uterine contents are forced to accumulate—uterine retention of dead eggs and egg remnants is sufficient for exopher elevation if the egg laying apparatus is defective.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Expansion of the uterine compartment, rather than eggshell/embryo integrity, tracks with exopher elevation.
claims.source: Expansion of the uterine compartment, rather than eggshell/embryo integrity, tracks with exopher elevation.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figures 6A and 6B.

claims.claim: Unfertilized oocytes cannot initiate embryonic development or egg-shell biosynthesis.
claims.source: Unfertilized oocytes cannot initiate embryonic development or egg-shell biosynthesis; nor can oocytes elevate ALMR exophergenesis in hermaphrodites that are proficient at egg-laying (Figure 1G&H).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of C. elegans reproductive biology.

claims.claim: Oocytes cannot elevate ALMR exophergenesis in hermaphrodites that are proficient at egg-laying.
claims.source: Unfertilized oocytes cannot initiate embryonic development or egg-shell biosynthesis; nor can oocytes elevate ALMR exophergenesis in hermaphrodites that are proficient at egg-laying (Figure 1G&H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1G and 1H.

claims.claim: In the absence of sperm, oocytes do not mature but are 'ovulated' at a reduced rate compared to in the presence of sperm.
claims.source: Note that in the absence of sperm, oocytes do not mature but are 'ovulated' at a reduced rate compared to in the presence of sperm; oogenesis continues such that ~25 oocytes are typically found stacked in the gonad (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; McGovern et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation (McGovern et al., 2007) and observations in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Oogenesis continues in the absence of sperm such that approximately 25 oocytes are typically found stacked in the gonad.
claims.source: Note that in the absence of sperm, oocytes do not mature but are 'ovulated' at a reduced rate compared to in the presence of sperm; oogenesis continues such that ~25 oocytes are typically found stacked in the gonad (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; McGovern et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation (McGovern et al., 2007) and observations in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Build-up of retained oocytes in egg-laying blocked animals was both sufficient to elevate exophers and expand the uterus.
claims.source: For both genetic retention strategies, we found that build-up of retained oocytes in egg-laying blocked animals was both sufficient to elevate exophers (Figure 6C&E) and expand the uterus (Figure 6D&F; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6C-F.

claims.claim: The oocyte retention was similarly efficacious in elevating exopher production to egg retention, increasing ALMR exophergenesis to approximately 80% in the sem-2(rf) mutant.
claims.source: Moreover, the oocyte retention was similarly efficacious in elevating exopher production to egg retention, increasing ALMR exophergenesis to approximately 80% in the sem-2(rf) mutant (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Fertilization, egg shells, and egg remnants are not essential for the early adult exopher peak.
claims.source: We conclude that fertilization, egg shells, and egg remnants are not essential for the early adult exopher peak.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figures 6C and 6E showing high exophers with oocyte retention.

claims.claim: Expansion of the uterus with unfertilized oocytes can suffice to elevate neuronal exopher formation.
claims.source: Expansion of the uterus with unfertilized oocytes can suffice to elevate neuronal exopher formation.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figures 6C-F.

claims.claim: lin-39 RNAi + oocyte retention promotes exopher formation, but eliminating oocytes (fem-3(gf)) eliminates exopher elevation even when egg-laying is blocked by lin-39 RNAi.
claims.source: lin-39 RNAi + oocyte retention promotes exopher formation, but eliminating oocytes (fem-3(gf)) eliminates exopher elevation even when egg-laying is blocked by lin-39 RNAi.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: Although oocyte accumulation with uterine expansion suffices to elevate exophers, removing the oocytes and uterus occupancy eliminates the exopher boost.
claims.source: That is to say, although oocyte accumulation with uterine expansion suffices to elevate exophers, removing the oocytes and uterus occupancy eliminates the exopher boost.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: Disruption of egg laying on its own is not the driving factor in high exophergenesis; rather, uterine filling is required.
claims.source: Thus, disruption of egg laying on its own is not the driving factor in high exophergenesis; rather, uterine filling is required.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figures 6G and 6H showing that blocking egg-laying without uterine filling does not induce exophers.

claims.claim: ALMR exophergenesis is strongly correlated with the level of uterus stretching caused by the accumulation of uterine contents.
claims.source: We revisited the relationship of uterine length and exopher level by adding data from the studies with oocyte retention to reinforce the conclusion that ALMR exophergenesis is strongly correlated with the level of uterus stretching caused by the accumulation of uterine contents (Figure 6I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6I demonstrating correlation between uterine length and exopher levels.

claims.claim: When 2 or more minutes of injection pressure was held continuously, approximately 20% of the ALMs scored exhibited an exopher event shortly after injection.
claims.source: We found that when we held injection pressure continuously for 2 or more minutes, ~20% of the ALMs scored exhibited an exopher event shortly after injection (Figure 7C&D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7C and 7D.

claims.claim: Injection experiments using animals with functional vulvae (in which injected material is rapidly extruded through the vulval opening) failed to induce ALMR exophers.
claims.source: Injection experiments using animals with functional vulvae (in which injected material is rapidly extruded through the vulval opening) failed to induce ALMR exophers (Figure 7E), supporting that ALMR exophergenesis caused by 2 min injection of dye-containing M9 is due to the physical distortion of gonad rather than the chemical impact of the dye-containing M9.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: ALMR exophergenesis caused by 2 min injection of dye-containing M9 is due to the physical distortion of gonad rather than the chemical impact of the dye-containing M9.
claims.source: Injection experiments using animals with functional vulvae (in which injected material is rapidly extruded through the vulval opening) failed to induce ALMR exophers (Figure 7E), supporting that ALMR exophergenesis caused by 2 min injection of dye-containing M9 is due to the physical distortion of gonad rather than the chemical impact of the dye-containing M9.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Exopher induction by uterine accumulation of eggs, malformed eggs, dead embryos, oocytes, or fluid-induced expansion supports a model in which early adult ALMR exophergenesis is elevated by physical distortion of the uterus that occurs with reproduction.
claims.source: In sum, exopher induction by uterine accumulation of eggs, malformed eggs, dead embryos, oocytes, or fluid-induced expansion supports a model in which early adult ALMR exophergenesis is elevated by physical distortion of the uterus that occurs with reproduction (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the cumulative experimental data in Figures 6 and 7.

claims.claim: The early exophergenesis peak is dependent on uterine occupation, which normally is conferred by fertilized egg accumulation prior to the deposition of eggs.
claims.source: Here, we report that the early exophergenesis peak is dependent on uterine occupation, which normally is conferred by fertilized egg accumulation prior to the deposition of eggs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the cumulative experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: Uterine expansion that is associated with the filling of a blocked uterus with unfertilized oocytes or by fluid alone can also induce high neuronal exopher production.
claims.source: Uterine expansion that is associated with the filling of a blocked uterus with unfertilized oocytes or by fluid alone can also induce high neuronal exopher production, supporting a model in which the physical distention associated with uterine occupancy, rather than chemical signals derived from fertilized eggs per se, is a required component of the signaling relay between reproduction and young adult neuronal debris elimination.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 6 and 7.

claims.claim: The physical distention associated with uterine occupancy, rather than chemical signals derived from fertilized eggs per se, is a required component of the signaling relay between reproduction and young adult neuronal debris elimination.
claims.source: Uterine expansion that is associated with the filling of a blocked uterus with unfertilized oocytes or by fluid alone can also induce high neuronal exopher production, supporting a model in which the physical distention associated with uterine occupancy, rather than chemical signals derived from fertilized eggs per se, is a required component of the signaling relay between reproduction and young adult neuronal debris elimination.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figures 6 and 7.

claims.claim: Trans-tissue cross-talk to the maternal nervous system appears accomplished via mechanical force transduction.
claims.source: Trans-tissue cross-talk to the maternal nervous system thus appears accomplished via mechanical force transduction.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the cumulative experimental data showing mechanical force effects on exopher production.

claims.claim: C. elegans reproduction features physical expansion and contraction of multiple tissue/cell types--the gonad houses the expanding germline, and the spermatheca expands and retracts vigorously as each mature oocyte enters and exits.
claims.source: C. elegans reproduction features physical expansion and contraction of multiple tissue/cell types--the gonad houses the expanding germline, and the spermatheca expands and retracts vigorously as each mature oocyte enters and exits.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of C. elegans reproductive biology.

claims.claim: The uterus stretches to house eggs and can contract locally as eggs transit or are expelled via the action of the vulval and uterine muscles.
claims.source: The uterus also stretches to house eggs and can contract locally as eggs transit or are expelled via the action of the vulval and uterine muscles.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of C. elegans reproductive biology.

claims.claim: The filled reproductive apparatus can exert both constitutive and sporadic pressure on surrounding tissues as it enacts its essential functions.
claims.source: The filled reproductive apparatus can thus clearly exert both constitutive and sporadic pressure on surrounding tissues as it enacts its essential functions.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from observations of tissue distortion by eggs and knowledge of reproductive mechanics.

claims.claim: Elegant work on the egg-laying circuit has provided evidence for mechanical signaling within the egg-laying circuit that regulates initiation, promotion, and termination of egg-laying.
claims.source: Elegant work on the egg-laying circuit (comprising the somatic gonad, the HSN and VC neurons, and the vulval, and uterine muscle) has provided evidence for mechanical signaling within the egg-laying circuit that regulates initiation, promotion, and termination of egg-laying (Medrano and Collins, 2023; Ravi et al., 2018; Kopchock et al., 2021; Ravi et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Medrano and Collins, 2023; Ravi et al., 2018; Kopchock et al., 2021; Ravi et al., 2021).

claims.claim: Exopher-promoting force seems unlikely to derive from the vulva or vulval muscle contractions, since when these cells are genetically disrupted in lin-39 RNAi or in sem-2 mutants, high levels of exophers still are generated.
claims.source: Working backward, exopher-promoting force seems unlikely to derive from the vulva or vulval muscle contractions, since when these cells are genetically disrupted in lin-39 RNAi or in sem-2 mutants, high levels of exophers still are generated.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figures 3 and 6 showing high exophers in vulva-defective mutants.

claims.claim: Spermatheca contractions are reported to be normal in hyperactive egg-laying goa-1.
claims.source: Changes in spermatheca volume, which expands and contracts dramatically as mature oocytes enter via valve opening/closure (Tan and Zaidel-Bar, 2015), might be sensed, but spermatheca contractions are reported to be normal in hyperactive egg-laying goa-1 (Govindan et al., 2006), which is an exopher-suppressing background.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Govindan et al., 2006).

claims.claim: Under no-sperm conditions, oocyte transit rates are lower than for fertilized eggs.
claims.source: Under no-sperm conditions, oocyte transit rates are lower than for fertilized eggs, and sperm-derived signals influence spermathecal valve opening (McGovern et al., 2007; McCarter et al., 1999; Miller et al., 2001), but if the egg-laying apparatus is genetically compromised and oocytes accumulate in the absence of sperm, exopher levels are high, suggesting deficits in spermatheca operations or sperm signals per se do not drive exophergenesis.

results.result: Exopher production from ALMR neurons peaks at adult day 2-3, coinciding with C. elegans reproductive peak. Treatment with FUdR, which blocks reproduction, suppresses this early adult exopher peak.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C32 are supported by temporal data in Figure 1B showing parallel peaks. Claims C35-C36 demonstrate FUdR suppression (Figure 1C) with appropriate statistical testing (p<0.001). The correlation is well-established, though causality requires additional experiments.

results.result: Genetic elimination of the germline using temperature-sensitive glp-4(bn2ts) mutants significantly reduces ALMR exopher production during the early adult peak period.
results.evaluation: Claim C40 correctly describes the glp-4(ts) system (supported by citation). Claim C41 is supported by experimental data in Figure 1E with appropriate temperature controls and statistical significance. The experimental design properly controls for temperature effects.

results.result: Oocytes are required for early adult ALMR exopher production. In fem-3(q20ts) mutants that produce only sperm but no oocytes, exophergenesis is mostly diminished over the first five days of adulthood.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1F using appropriate temperature-sensitive controls. Claims C45-C46 represent reasonable inferences from the data. The conclusion that sperm alone are insufficient is well-supported by the genetic evidence.

results.result: Functional sperm are required for early adult ALMR exopher production. Blocking spermatogenesis using fem-1(lf) mutants or SPE-44 degradation via AID system abolishes ALMR exopher production.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49 are supported by experimental data in Figures 1G-H using two independent genetic approaches. Claims C50-C51 represent reasonable inferences. The dual requirement for both sperm and oocytes is well-established, though the mechanism remains unclear.

results.result: Disruption of eggshell biosynthesis genes or genes required for 1-2 cell stage embryonic development causes potent suppression of ALMR exophergenesis, while disruption of later-stage embryonic genes has negligible impact. This suggests the exopher-inducing signal is associated with the earliest stages of embryonic development.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C59 are supported by RNAi data in Figures 2B-H. However, claim C61 acknowledges that eggshell formation and early cell divisions cannot be genetically separated, making claim C62 ambiguous. The inference in C60 is reasonable but the confounding of eggshell integrity with early embryonic events limits mechanistic conclusions.

results.result: Restoring egg production in reproductively senescing hermaphrodites through mating with males extends the period of elevated exopher production. This demonstrates that the age-related decline in exophers is due to lack of eggs rather than chronological aging of neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are supported by experimental data in Figures 3A-B with appropriate controls (sterile vs. fertile males). Claims C67-C68 represent reasonable inferences from the rescue experiment. The experimental design effectively distinguishes between egg presence and chronological age as causal factors.

results.result: Genetic interventions that block egg-laying and induce egg retention (egl-9, egl-3, sem-2 mutants, lin-39 RNAi) dramatically elevate ALMR exopher production. This effect occurs regardless of transgene expression level (multi-copy vs. single-copy) and is consistent across different genetic strategies.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C73 are supported by experimental data in Figures 3D-H using multiple independent genetic approaches with appropriate statistical testing. Claim C74 is supported by comparison of multi-copy and single-copy transgenes (Figures 3G-H). The consistency across approaches strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Pharmacological and genetic manipulation of egg-laying behavior modulates exopher production. Octopamine (promotes egg retention) enhances exophers, serotonin (promotes egg-laying) suppresses exophers, and goa-1 mutants (hyperactive egg-laying) show reduced exophers. Overall, uterine egg occupancy strongly correlates with exopher levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3I, though the 5-HT experiment uses fasting conditions which adds complexity. Claim C81 is supported by Figure 3J. Claim C82 represents a reasonable synthesis of the cumulative data. The correlation is well-established across multiple experimental paradigms.

results.result: ALMR soma positioning within the egg zone strongly correlates with exopher production. Among neurons that produced exophers, 95% (36/37) were positioned within the egg zone, compared to 70% (63/91) of neurons that did not produce exophers (p<0.01).
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 establish the anatomical context (supported by citations and EM data in Figure 4B). Claims C86-C88 are supported by positional analysis in Figure 4D with appropriate statistical testing. However, the correlation does not establish causality, and the 70% baseline positioning in the egg zone for non-exopher neurons suggests additional factors are involved.

results.result: Genetic manipulation of ALM neuron positioning using a mec-3 promoter fragment demonstrates that neurons positioned anterior to AVM (away from eggs) show dramatically reduced exopher production (~5%, 4/73) compared to posterior positioning (~71%, 55/78). This supports a model where proximity to the egg-filled uterus drives exopher production.
results.evaluation: Claim C89 is supported by citation (Toms et al., 2001). Claim C91 shows dramatic positional effects (Figure 4F). However, claim C90 reveals an unexpected high baseline (~40%) in rol-6 animals, which is a confounding factor not adequately addressed. The rol-6 mutation affects cuticle structure and could independently influence exopher production, making it difficult to attribute effects solely to position.

results.result: In sem-2(rf) mutants with expanded uteri, multiple touch neurons (ALML, AVM, PVM) that are normally positioned near the expanded uterus increase exopher production, while posterior PLM neurons that cannot be approached by the gonad do not produce exophers.
results.evaluation: Claim C92 is supported by experimental data in Figure 4G showing differential effects on different touch neurons based on their proximity to the expanded uterus. This provides strong evidence that proximity to the egg-filled region is a key factor, though it remains correlative rather than demonstrating direct mechanical force.

results.result: Genetic interventions that promote exopher production are associated with expanded uterus lengths, while interventions that suppress exophers are associated with shorter uterus lengths. However, not all developmental compromises cause uterine extension, as mex-3 and gad-1 RNAi (which don't affect exophers) show normal uterine length.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 are supported by uterine length measurements in Figures 5B-H with appropriate statistical testing. Claim C100 is supported by Figure 5H showing that not all embryonic disruptions cause uterine extension. The correlation between uterine length and exopher production is well-established, though the measurements are absolute rather than normalized to body length.

results.result: Uterine retention of dead eggs and egg remnants (via cbd-1 RNAi in sem-2(rf) background) is sufficient to elevate exopher production (~45%) despite disrupted eggshell formation and embryonic development. This demonstrates that intact eggshells and early embryonic divisions are not required for exopher induction when the uterus is expanded.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C104 are supported by experimental data in Figures 6A-B showing high exophers and expanded uterus in cbd-1 RNAi; sem-2(rf) animals. Claims C105-C107 represent reasonable inferences. This is a critical experiment that begins to distinguish between chemical signals from viable embryos versus physical distention.

results.result: Accumulation of unfertilized oocytes in egg-laying blocked animals (sem-2(rf) or lin-39 RNAi with SPE-44 AID) is sufficient to elevate exophers (~80% in sem-2(rf)) and expand the uterus. This demonstrates that fertilization, eggshells, and embryonic development are not essential for exopher induction.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C113 are supported by experimental data in Figures 6C-F showing high exophers and expanded uterus with oocyte retention. Claims C114-C115 represent reasonable inferences from this critical experiment. This strongly supports the mechanical distention hypothesis over chemical signaling from embryos.

results.result: Blocking egg-laying without uterine filling (lin-39 RNAi + fem-3(gf) to eliminate oocytes, or sem-2(rf) + cbd-1 RNAi + fem-3(gf)) does not induce exophers. This demonstrates that disruption of egg-laying alone is insufficient; uterine filling is required.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C117 are supported by experimental data in Figures 6G-H showing that removing uterine contents eliminates exopher elevation even when egg-laying is blocked. Claim C118 represents a reasonable inference. This is a critical control experiment that strengthens the uterine filling hypothesis.

results.result: ALMR exophergenesis is strongly correlated with uterine length across multiple genetic conditions, as demonstrated by correlation analysis (Pearson r = 0.8839, p = 0.0003).
results.evaluation: Claim C119 is supported by correlation analysis in Figure 6I combining data from multiple experiments. The strong correlation (r = 0.8839) with high statistical significance supports the uterine distention model. However, correlation does not establish causation, and the analysis would benefit from normalization to body length.

results.result: Sustained microinjection of M9 buffer into the uterus for 2+ minutes induces ALMR exophers in ~20% of vulvaless animals within 10 minutes. Injection into animals with functional vulvae (where fluid is rapidly expelled) fails to induce exophers, supporting that physical distortion rather than chemical effects drives exopher production.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C121 are supported by experimental data in Figures 7C-E. Claim C122 represents a reasonable inference from the vulva control experiment. This is the most direct test of the mechanical force hypothesis, though the ~20% induction rate is modest and the injection contains dye which could have effects beyond mechanical distention.

results.result: The authors conclude that mechanical force from uterine distention, rather than chemical signals from fertilized eggs, is the primary driver of early adult exopher production. This conclusion is based on the ability of eggs, dead eggs, oocytes, and fluid injection to induce exophers when the uterus is distended.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C126 represent the central conclusion of the manuscript, supported by cumulative evidence from Figures 1-7. However, while the evidence strongly supports a role for mechanical force, it does not definitively exclude chemical signaling. The experiments show that mechanical distention is sufficient but do not prove it is necessary or that chemical signals play no role. The injection experiment (C14) provides the most direct evidence but has limitations (modest induction rate, potential chemical effects of dye).

These provide context for discussing potential mechanotransduction mechanisms.

results.result: Discussion claims about the source of exopher-promoting force, arguing against vulva, vulval muscle, and spermatheca as primary sources based on genetic evidence, and proposing that a filled uterus is the simplest model.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C136 represent reasonable inferences from the experimental data (Figures 3, 6). Claim C137 represents a synthesis of the evidence. The logic is sound, though alternative explanations are not exhaustively tested.

results.result: Discussion of potential mechanotransduction mechanisms, including ion channels (Piezo, TRP, DEG/ENaC), adhesion GPCRs, and YAP/TAZ signaling, with speculation about which might be most appropriate for sustained uterine forces.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C139 are supported by established knowledge and citation (Delmas and Coste, 2013). Claims C140-C142 are supported by citations (Mee et al., 2004; Willson et al., 2004; Hutter et al., 2000; Panciera et al., 2017) and represent reasonable speculation about potential mechanisms. These are appropriately presented as hypotheses for future work.

results.result: Discussion of the rapid timeframe of exopher induction after fluid injection (10 min after 2 min injection), suggesting that proteostressed touch neurons are poised to eliminate contents upon mechanical stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claim C143 is supported by experimental data in Figure 7. Claim C144 represents a reasonable inference from the rapid response. This observation has implications for understanding the mechanotransduction mechanism.

results.result: Discussion of mechanical signaling in reproduction across species, including Drosophila reproductive tract distention affecting maternal behavior (via PPK1 channel) and mammalian uterine stretch influencing maternal behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C147 are supported by citations (Gou et al., 2014; Kristal, 2009). These provide comparative context suggesting that mechanosensing in reproduction may be broadly conserved.

results.result: Discussion of muscle exophers in C. elegans (Turek et al., 2021) showing similar temporal patterns and egg-dependence, leading to speculation that reproduction triggers a 'license' for EV/exopher production across tissues, potentially conferring selective advantage for maternal reproduction.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C149 are supported by citation (Turek et al., 2021). Claims C150-C152 are explicitly speculative. While the parallel with muscle exophers is interesting, the speculation about tissue-wide licensing and selective advantage goes beyond the data and would require additional experimental support.

results.result: Discussion of proteostasis reorganization in early adult C. elegans, including HSF-1 downregulation, enhanced proteasome activity, and speculation that exopher-mediated elimination represents another branch of this reconfiguration. The HSF-1 downregulation is blocked by cbd-1 RNAi, suggesting eggs signal across tissues.
results.evaluation: Claims C153-C155 are supported by citations (Labbadia and Morimoto, 2014, 2015; Sala and Morimoto, 2022; Sala et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2011). Claim C157 is supported by citation (Sala et al., 2020). However, claims C156, C158-C159 are speculative and go beyond the data. The connection between HSF-1 regulation and exopher production is not directly tested in this manuscript.

results.result: Discussion of temporal 'clean up' phases in development, noting that exophers are not observed in larval stages and speculating about programmed proteome clean-up at developmental transitions, with examples from oocyte maturation and neuronal stem cell quiescence exit.
results.evaluation: Claim C160 is supported by citation (Melentijevic et al., 2017). Claims C164-C165 are supported by citations (Bohnert and Kenyon, 2017; Morrow et al., 2020). Claims C161-C163 are speculative but represent reasonable hypotheses based on the temporal patterns observed. The speculation is appropriately qualified.

results.result: Discussion of mechanical stress and exopher-like vesicle production in mammalian systems (cardiomyocytes, kidney epithelial cells) and the general influence of biomechanical force on EV biogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C167 are supported by citations (Nicolás-Ávila et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2023). Claims C168-C169 are supported by citation (Thompson and Papoutsakis, 2023) and represent accurate characterization of the field. These provide broader context for the mechanobiology findings.

results.result: Discussion of mechanical stress in neurodegeneration, including links between traumatic brain injury/hypertension/hydrocephalus and Alzheimer's pathology, with examples of mechanical effects on APP/β-secretase expression and microglial Piezo1 mechanosensing. The authors conclude their study reveals mechanical force can influence neuronal release of vesicles containing neurotoxic species.
results.evaluation: Claims C170, C172-C173 are supported by citations (Ramos-Cejudo et al., 2018; Malone et al., 2022; Gangoda et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2023). Claim C171 is speculative but reasonable. Claim C174 is supported by the cumulative experimental data in the manuscript. The connection to neurodegenerative disease is appropriately qualified as inviting further consideration.

results.result: Exopher production from the C. elegans ALMR neuron peaks at adult day 2 or 3, coinciding with the C. elegans reproductive peak. This temporal pattern represents a key observation about the timing of exopher production in relation to reproduction.
results.evaluation: All reviewers accept this finding without question. Reviewer 2 states 'the frequency of exopher production correlates with the timing of reproduction' and Reviewer 3 notes 'the evidence that egg accumulation leads to exopher production is strong.' The temporal correlation is treated as a well-established observation.

results.result: Genetic disruption of C. elegans germline, sperm, oocytes, or early embryo production strongly suppresses exopher extrusion from ALMR neurons during the peak period. Multiple genetic approaches (glp-4, fem-1, fem-3, SPE-44 AID, FUdR treatment) demonstrate that both functional sperm and oocytes are required for exopher production.
results.evaluation: Reviewers unanimously accept these findings. Reviewer 2 states 'The genetic data presented is thorough and solid' and Reviewer 3 notes 'the experiments are very convincing, using a battery of RNAi and mutant approaches to distinguish direct from indirect effects.' The systematic genetic dissection is praised as methodologically sound.

results.result: Restoring egg production through late-life mating or inducing egg retention via genetic/pharmacological interventions that block egg-laying strongly increases ALMR exopher production. Multiple approaches (mating, egl mutants, lin-39 RNAi, octopamine/serotonin treatment, goa-1 mutants) demonstrate that uterine egg occupancy correlates with exopher levels.
results.evaluation: All reviewers strongly support these findings. Reviewer 3 states 'Shifting the timing of egg production and egg laying alters the onset of observed exophers. Pharmacological manipulation of egg laying has the predicted effects, with animals retaining fewer eggs having fewer exophers and animals with increased egg accumulation having more.' The complementary approaches are viewed as convincing.

results.result: Disruption of eggshell biosynthesis genes or genes required for 1-2 cell stage embryonic development causes potent suppression of ALMR exophergenesis, while disruption of later-stage embryonic development genes has negligible impact. This suggests the exopher-inducing signal is associated with the earliest stages of embryonic development.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding as part of the systematic genetic dissection. Reviewer 3 notes the experiments 'distinguish direct from indirect effects' and the temporal specificity of the requirement is consistent with the overall model. No concerns are raised about these specific genetic manipulations.

results.result: In a single-copy mKate transgenic strain (low exogenous protein expression), egg retention induced by lin-39 RNAi drives approximately 60% exophergenesis, similar to the multi-copy transgene strain, demonstrating that egg retention can induce high exopher production regardless of exogenous protein expression levels.
results.evaluation: This finding directly addresses a major concern raised by reviewers. Reviewer 2 states 'The authors have addressed the main weakness of the study in the revised manuscript, by providing data showing stimulation of exopher production in a single-copy transgenic line.' Reviewer 3 notes 'The authors have now included data from strains bearing a single-copy transgene...showing that induced egg accumulation drives a similar degree of exopher production. This indicates that exposers seen are generated in response to specific biological conditions and not merely an artifact of mCherry protein over-expression.'

results.result: Genetic interventions that promote ALMR exopher production are associated with expanded uterus lengths, while interventions that suppress exopher production are associated with shorter uterus lengths. ALMR exophergenesis is strongly correlated with the level of uterus stretching caused by accumulation of uterine contents.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this correlation as part of the evidence for mechanical force. Reviewer 3 states 'The authors show that egg production and accumulation have dramatic consequences to the viscera' and the correlation between uterine length and exopher production is treated as supporting evidence for the mechanical model.

results.result: ALMR soma positioning in the vicinity of eggs correlates with exopher production: 95% of exopher-producing ALMRs were positioned within the egg zone, and experimentally moving ALM neurons away from eggs dramatically reduces exopher production. In egg-retention mutants, multiple touch neurons near the expanded uterus produce exophers, while posterior neurons distant from the gonad do not.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly support this spatial correlation. Reviewer 3 states 'moving the ALMR process away from eggs prevents the formation of exophers. This effect is not unique to ALMR but is also observed in other touch neurons, with a clear bias toward neurons whose cell bodies are adjacent to the filled uterus.' The spatial relationship is viewed as key evidence for mechanical force.

results.result: ALMR exopher production can be enhanced by filling the uterus with oocytes, dead eggs, or fluid, demonstrating that intact eggshells and embryonic development are not required. Uterine expansion with unfertilized oocytes or dead embryos (when egg-laying is blocked) is sufficient to elevate exopher production, supporting that uterine distention rather than fertilized egg-specific signals drives exopher induction.
results.evaluation: All reviewers strongly support this finding as critical evidence for the mechanical model. Reviewer 3 states 'Embryos lacking an intact eggshell with reduced rigidity have impaired exopher production' and 'the experiments provide convincing evidence that exopher production is driven by stretch-dependent feedback of fertilized, intact eggs in the adult uterus.' The ability of various uterine contents to induce exophers is viewed as key evidence.

results.result: Microinjection of fluid into the uterus for 2 or more minutes induces exopher production in approximately 20% of ALMs within 10 minutes, and this effect requires sustained pressure (injection in animals with functional vulvae fails to induce exophers). This demonstrates that physical distortion rather than chemical signals causes exopher induction.
results.evaluation: Reviewers view this as strong direct evidence for mechanical force. Reviewer 3 states 'The microinjection experiment is very interesting, and the authors have added additional details on how these experiments were conducted in the revised manuscript' and 'Acute injection into the uterus to mimic the stretch that accompanies egg production causes a similar induction of exopher release.' The control with functional vulvae is noted as supporting the mechanical interpretation.

results.result: The mechanical force of uterine occupation potentiates exopher extrusion from proximal proteostressed maternal neurons. Physical distention associated with uterine occupancy, rather than chemical signals from fertilized eggs, is the required component of signaling between reproduction and neuronal debris elimination, accomplished via mechanical force transduction.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly support this central conclusion. The editor states 'The authors provide compelling evidence to support the idea that uterine distension per se can induce vesicular extrusion from adjacent neurons.' Reviewer 2 concludes 'communication between the uterus and proximal neurons occurs through the sensing of mechanic forces of expansion normally provided by egg occupancy.' Reviewer 3 states 'Together these results are consistent with a model where stretch caused by fertilized embryo accumulation, and not chemical signals from the eggs themselves or egg release, underlies ALMR exopher production.'

results.result: Background claims about exopher biology: C. elegans neurons extrude ~5 μm vesicles called exophers that carry deleterious proteins/organelles; proteostasis disruption increases exopher production; exophers can be neuroprotective; exopher contents are transferred to hypodermal cells; similar biology exists in mammals; exophers are generated only in adults with peaks at days 2-3 and later ages.
results.evaluation: These background claims are accepted without question by all reviewers as they are based on prior published work. They provide context for the current study but are not the focus of reviewer evaluation.

results.result: Background knowledge claims about C. elegans reproductive biology, egg-laying circuits, mechanotransduction mechanisms, and established genetic/pharmacological tools. These include details about FUdR function, germline development, fertilization timing, egg-laying regulation, and mechanosensory channels.
results.evaluation: These are established facts from prior literature that reviewers accept without question. They provide necessary biological context but are not novel findings being evaluated.

results.result: Eggs can readily be observed to distort tissue structure in young adult C. elegans, and the filled reproductive apparatus can exert constitutive and sporadic pressure on surrounding tissues including touch neurons.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these observational claims as supporting evidence for the mechanical model. Reviewer 3 notes 'The authors show that egg production and accumulation have dramatic consequences to the viscera.' These observations are treated as straightforward documentation of tissue distortion.

results.result: Mechanistic inferences about the source of mechanical force: exopher-promoting force is unlikely to derive from vulva/vulval muscle contractions (since disrupting these still allows high exophers); deficits in spermatheca operations or sperm signals per se do not drive exophergenesis; the simplest model is that a filled uterus is sensed and required for exopher production.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these inferences as reasonable interpretations of the genetic data. The logic of ruling out alternative sources of mechanical force is viewed as sound, though reviewers note the molecular mechanism remains unknown.

results.result: Discussion and speculation about: potential mechanotransduction mechanisms (ion channels, GPCRs, YAP/TAZ); rapid timeframe of exopher induction; comparison to fly reproductive tract mechanosensing; proteostasis reorganization in early adulthood; evolutionary advantages; broader implications for EV biology and neurodegeneration; mechanical stress in other systems.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these as reasonable discussion points and speculation. Reviewer 4 explicitly notes 'The main weakness of the paper is that it does not explore the molecular mechanism by which the mechanical signals are received or responded to by the neuron. The authors are currently addressing this in their follow-up studies.' This indicates reviewers view the mechanistic speculation as appropriate for discussion but recognize it as future work.

results.result: Speculative claims about broader significance: large vesicle extrusion may contribute to spreading pathogenic aggregates and inflammatory responses in neurodegeneration; the basic transfer biology may represent a conserved process for animal-wide proteostasis balance.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises uncertainty about the biological significance, stating 'Whether this process is related to the extrusion of cellular damage by the neurons in relatively young day 2 animals should be addressed in future studies.' This suggests reviewers view the connection to pathology and the functional significance as uncertain and requiring further investigation.

OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to confounding of eggshell integrity with early embryonic events (C61), while peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting it as part of the systematic genetic approach without raising the confounding concern.

OpenEval emphasizes the experimental design distinguishing egg presence from chronological age, while peer reviewers note this as part of evidence that 'shifting the timing of egg production and egg laying alters the onset of observed exophers.'
